name: DIRECT
tagline: Wisconsin's late-1970s multiprocessor database machine, and the project that produced the Wisconsin Benchmark.
description: DIRECT was a relational database machine built at the University of Wisconsin-Madison by David DeWitt's group and first described at ISCA in 1978 (with a fuller IEEE Transactions on Computers paper in 1979). A controller decomposed relational queries into operators on fixed-size pages and assigned them dynamically to a pool of query processors that shared a bank of page-sized memory modules, so intra-query and inter-query parallelism came from the same mechanism. Benchmarking it against commercial systems led to the Wisconsin Benchmark, which embarrassed several vendors and shaped database benchmarking for a decade. DIRECT itself was never a product; its lessons fed directly into DeWitt's shared-nothing Gamma machine and, through it, today's parallel SQL engines.
statusNote: Research prototype (c. 1978-1984) at UW-Madison; ideas carried into Gamma and later shared-nothing parallel databases.
developer: University of Wisconsin-Madison (David DeWitt et al.)

pricing.notes: Never sold or distributed; only the papers are available.

scale.notes: Parallelism came from adding query processors that shared page-sized memory modules.

queryLanguages: Relational query trees issued by a host system
strengths: Early demonstration of page-level, dynamically scheduled intra- and inter-query parallelism
Origin of the Wisconsin Benchmark, a template for later database benchmarks
Well-documented in ISCA 1978 and IEEE ToC 1979 papers, useful for teaching database-machine history
weaknesses: Hardware prototype that was never released as software
Shared-memory design hit bandwidth limits that pushed the field to shared-nothing (Gamma)
useCases: Studying the history of parallel query execution
Teaching the database-machine era and why it gave way to shared-nothing clusters
Background for understanding the Wisconsin Benchmark
notIdealFor: Anything beyond study: there is no runnable system
